name: Pines — 39 landscape-forming species
status: 5 archetypal species (full list archived in docs/plant_archive)
notes: Kew accepts ~115 pines; these are the ones that make forests: boreal, Mediterranean, Himalayan, Chinese and Japanese, western and eastern North American, Mexican and Caribbean. Wind-pollinated; seeds by wind and by nutcrackers/jays (whitebark, Swiss stone, pinyon depend on birds). Many are fire species: lodgepole and jack pine reseed a burn in even-aged stands; longleaf and ponderosa need fire to keep their savanna open — the disturbance phase should read that.

canopy.name: Scots pine

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 5-7 cotyledons; in its first year it has single, flat, finely serrated primary needles 2-3 cm long, then short, twisted, blue-green paired needles. Young trees are regular, bushy cones; later the lower branches drop and the crown becomes flat or rounded above a tall trunk whose upper bark is orange and flaky.
growth.source: Wikipedia (to 35 m, over 45 m on the best sites; normally lives 150-300 years, over 760 in Lapland; first-year seedlings have single serrated leaves 2-3 cm; seeds released 22-24 months after pollination); growth and first cones from European yield tables

canopy.source: Eurasia, Scotland to Siberia; 20–35 m. Orange upper bark; the boreal and heath pine. Kew POWO for the name; standard floras for range.

canopy.name: Stone pine

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings have 10-13 cotyledons and for 5-10 years carry juvenile foliage: single, soft, silvery blue-green needles 2-4 cm long, making a bushy, rounded, bluish globe rather than a cone. Adult paired, stiff green needles gradually take over by about age 10; the tree then lifts into a flat umbrella crown on a bare trunk.
growth.source: Wikipedia (juvenile leaves for 5-10 years, fully adult by ~10; a bushy globe in youth, an umbrella in mid-age; 12-20 m typical, to 25+; cones take 36 months to mature, longest of any pine); first cones and lifespan estimated

canopy.source: Mediterranean coasts; 15–25 m. Umbrella crown; pine nuts. Kew POWO for the name; standard floras for range.

canopy.name: Ponderosa pine

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 6-12 cotyledons; in its first months it drives a taproot 50 cm deep while the shoot stays short, with single primary needles, then long needles in bundles of three. Saplings ('blackjacks') are narrow cones with dark grey-black bark and long, tufted, yellow-green needles; bark turns to orange puzzle-plates with age.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (Oliver & Ryker): first cones at age 7, most seed at 60-160 yrs; taproots reach 50+ cm within months; dominants grow 0.24-0.46 m/yr up to age 60; intolerant of shade; commonly lives 300-600 years

canopy.source: western North America; 30–50 m. Vanilla-scented orange plates; open parkland forest. Kew POWO for the name; standard floras for range.

canopy.name: Lodgepole pine

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 3-6 cotyledons and a tuft of single primary needles, then short, twisted, paired needles. Young trees are dense, narrow cones with regular whorls. Open-grown shore pines become bushy, crooked and flat-topped; inland trees become slim, straight poles. Serotinous cones stay closed on the branches for decades.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (Lotan & Critchfield): viable seed commonly at 5-10 years; ~3.6 m at 20 years on medium sites; germination peaks in the 2 weeks after snowmelt; very intolerant of shade; shore pine small and short-lived; ages commonly 150-200+, old high-elevation trees to 400+

canopy.source: western North American mountains; 20–35 m. Dense even-aged stands after fire; cones open in heat. Kew POWO for the name; standard floras for range.

canopy.name: Bristlecone pine

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 5-8 cotyledons, then short needles in dense bundles of five that stay 10-40 years, so even young twigs look like bristly foxtails. On harsh sites a 40-year-old may be only 15 cm tall. Old trees on wind-blasted dolomite are twisted, mostly dead snags of polished wood with a living strip of bark feeding a few branches.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Pinus longaeva: oldest living tree 5,062 years; seed immediately germinable; 40-year-olds 15 cm tall on extreme sites, ~2.5 cm of diameter per century at Wheeler Peak, faster on good sites; shade intolerant, cannot establish in dense forest. Age at first cones estimated

canopy.source: Great Basin high peaks; 5–15 m. Oldest trees on Earth; gnarled, half-dead giants. Kew POWO for the name; standard floras for range.
